facts.text: The eastern rosella is a parrot native to south-eastern Australia.
facts.quote: The eastern rosella (Platycercus eximius) is a parrot native and endemic to south-eastern Australia.

facts.text: The eastern rosella has white cheeks, a red head, a red upper breast, and a yellow lower breast that fades to pale green.
facts.quote: Its cheeks are white, and it has a red-coloured head. The beak is white, and the irises are brown. Its upper breast is red, and its lower breast is yellow and fades to pale green over the abdomen.

facts.text: The eastern rosella grows to 30 cm long.
facts.quote: The eastern rosella is 30 cm (12 in) long.

facts.text: The eastern rosella mostly feeds on grass seeds, buds, flowers, nectars, fruits, insects and larvae.
facts.quote: the eastern rosella mostly feeds on grass seeds, buds, flowers, nectars, fruits, as well as insects and their larvae.

facts.text: Eastern rosellas are reported to feed on 50 different plant species and 15 species of animals.
facts.quote: with reports of them feeding on 50 different plant species and 15 species of animals.

facts.text: In Australia, eastern rosellas usually breed from August to February, nesting in hollow trees and nest boxes.
facts.quote: In Australia, eastern rosellas usually breed in the austral summer from August to February. They are cavity nesters, and build their nests in the hollow trees and nest boxes.

facts.text: Female eastern rosellas lay 5 to 6 eggs on average, and the eggs are incubated for 18 to 22 days until hatching.
facts.quote: Female eastern rosellas lay 5 to 6 eggs on average, at intervals of 1 to 3 days. The eggs are usually laid in mid-November and mid-December and are incubated for 18 to 22 days until hatching.

facts.text: Eastern rosellas are highly territorial and may destroy the eggs of other rosellas nesting too close to their own nest.
facts.quote: Eastern rosellas can be highly territorial, and may destroy the eggs of conspecifics nesting too closely to their own nest.

facts.text: New Zealand's eastern rosellas became established after birds were released off Otago Heads around 1910, when Customs prohibited their entry.
facts.quote: Its first introduction occurred around 1910, when a small shipment of eastern rosellas, as well as a few crimson rosellas (P. elegans), was prohibited entry into New Zealand by the Customs Department. The birds were released off Otago Heads by the ship's crew before returning to Sydney.
